sources: Frontiers in Zoology 2024 (Barutia & Sombke), via research/74: "The trochanter exhibits a preferred breakage point."; "In the latter, the appendage is fully regenerated after one molt. This term was used for house centipedes."; this "allows these animals to easily lose legs in order to escape predators."; https://frontiersinzoology.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12983-024-00544-0

Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station fact sheet: antennae "similar in appearance to their legs, making it difficult for potential predators to tell which way it is facing"; "nocturnal and incredibly wary. Most that live in houses are never seen"; "will immediately flee if they are discovered"; "actively hunt other arthropods such as cockroach nymphs, bed bugs, flies, ants, silverfish, spiders"; "prefer cool, humid, dark environments"; https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/caes/documents/publications/fact_sheets/entomology/house_centipede_scutigera.pdf

Penn State Extension, House Centipedes: "one to one and one-half inches in length ... an overall appearance of being from three to four inches in length (including legs and antennae)"; "the last pair (on adult females) nearly twice the length of the body"; "In floor drains without water traps", "Under and in cardboard boxes", "crawl spaces"; "come out at night to forage for prey"; "may signify a greater problem than the presence of the centipedes"; sticky traps show which arthropods feed them; "Reduce the humidity"; https://extension.psu.edu/house-centipedes

University of Arkansas Arthropod Museum, House centipede: "They can capture several prey items at one time. They feed on one specimen while holding the others"; "jaws are not powerful enough to break human skin easily"; "Severe swelling and pain can result from the venom injected, but in most cases the bite is no worse than the sting of a bee"; https://arthropod.uark.edu/house-centipede/
CAES: a sting on a human is "very rare ... the result of rough handling" (research/74 fix C3: "Almost never. Mostly if you grab it.")

tiktok_title: House Centipede: The Leg It Drops and Where It Hides
tiktok_caption: house centipede in your bathroom 🐛 it can drop a leg to escape and usually regrows it by its next molt. Seeing lots of them may mean you have lots of other bugs. Stay or squish? 🐛✅ or 👟💥 #housecentipede #bugsinhouse #learnontiktok #thingslivinginyourhouse #meatballmyths

beats.say: Your bathroom bug can drop a fucking leg to escape you.
Each leg has a built-in fucking breaking point.
By its next molt, it usually grows that shit back. No fucking warranty needed.
Those long things up front? Fucking antennae that look like legs.
Predators struggle to tell which end is the fucking head. Same, honestly.
Its body is only a fucking inch or so long.
Legs and antennae make it look three to four inches. Like a fucking eyelash that learned to run.
Babies hatch with just eight legs. Cute little fuckers.
Growing up can take three years or more. Fucking late bloomer.
It hunts spiders, silverfish, cockroaches, even bed bugs. That's not a diet, that's a fucking hit list.
It can catch several fucking bugs at once.
It eats one while it holds the others. Fucking meal prep.
But here's where the fuck it hides while you're not looking.
Dry floor drains. Under cardboard boxes. Fucking crawl spaces.
The fucker comes out at night to hunt.
Turn on the light, and it hauls ass like it owes you fucking money.
Most house centipedes are never fucking seen at all.
Some fall into your tub at night and get trapped. All those legs, and some still get stuck in a fucking tub.
Seeing lots? Shit. You may have a bigger fucking bug problem.
They go where the fucking food is.
Dry the room. Fix leaks. Move the fucking cardboard.
It won't fucking harm your pets, clothes, or house.
It almost never bites. Mostly if you grab it. So don't grab the fucking thing.
Usually it's like a bee sting. That shit can still swell.
So. Stay or fucking squish? Don't lie.
